description: Drama Years 1-2 width tiers — ACARA v9. All strands are capability strands; primary axis is task_contexts.
subject: Drama

width_notes.minimum_width: The narrowest honest floor for the descriptor's command term. For Y1-2 Drama, minimum is one task context in which the student meets the command term — one role, one sharing context, one drama example observed.
width_notes.typical_width: Full descriptor scope grounded in elaborations — the range of contexts a well-taught Y1-2 class would engage with across a unit.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions adding new task types, cultural contexts, or imaginative scenarios — not harder versions of the same task.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations used as primary source data. First Nations elaborations appear in wider for E02 (which is entirely First Nations focused) and in wider for other standards where elaborations indicate First Nations connections.

AC9ADR2C01.minimum_width: Student creates or co-creates one fictional situation with at least one other person, using non-verbal or verbal communication to establish role and situation.
AC9ADR2C01.typical_width: Students create and co-create fictional situations through dramatic play, process drama and puppetry; they contribute ideas and actions in group improvisations; they use facial expressions, movement, costume items and props to establish roles; they work with teacher-in-role and in Readers' Theatre contexts.
wider: Students use puppets they have made from repurposed or recycled materials to create new stories, including stories modelled on puppets from Asian cultures
Students devise short scenes communicating their connection to and responsibility for a place in their community, drawing on First Nations Australians' drama about Country/Place
Students use inquiry questions to propose and extend fictional situations ('What might happen next? What if I was there?')
Students co-create fictional spaces using unstructured materials and everyday clothing items to symbolise roles
elaborations: using puppets to create new stories, including stories that communicate understanding of existing stories or personal experiences
using learning from explorations of First Nations Australians' drama to devise drama communicating connection to place
using costume items and props to share character information in Readers' Theatre
identifying situations from stories, films, fantasy, history or personal experience to explore through dramatic play
contributing ideas within whole group or small group improvisations including teacher-in-role
communicating non-verbally using facial expressions and movements to explore role and situation in mime
accepting or developing the pretence situation established by others

AC9ADR2D01.minimum_width: Student uses at least two elements of drama (from: role, place, situation, language, movement) intentionally in a dramatic play or process drama sequence, and can name them.
AC9ADR2D01.typical_width: Students understand and use drama terminology; they take on roles purposefully, staying in role during improvised drama; they develop ideas from texts and images; they use familiar props and materials; they explore language, voice and movement in creating roles and situations.
wider: Students explore how manipulating one element (e.g. changing place, adding a new character) transforms a dramatic situation
Students explore mime and movement-based drama without voice, discovering how movement communicates role and situation independently
Students participate in process drama with teacher-in-role, exploring how the teacher's character shapes the unfolding fictional world
elaborations: exploring a situation through dramatic play using familiar props
understanding and employing appropriate drama terminology
taking part in purposeful dramatic play focusing on creating roles and situations
taking turns offering and accepting ideas, and staying in role during improvised drama
brainstorming and discussing situations from experiences and using these ideas to improvise drama

AC9ADR2E01.minimum_width: Student identifies at least two contexts where drama is experienced (beyond the classroom) and explains one reason why people in a specific context make and experience drama.
AC9ADR2E01.typical_width: Students share experiences of drama in school, community and home contexts; they recognise that drama communicates feelings and ideas; they ask and discuss questions about how and why drama is made; they explore how drama communicates cultural knowledge in their own and other communities.
wider: Students investigate drama from a country or region in Asia, exploring what it communicates and why it matters to that community
Students compare two drama contexts from different cultures, identifying similarities and differences in purpose, form and audience relationship
Students explore how drama communicates cultural knowledge through community ceremonies, celebrations and storytelling traditions
elaborations: identifying where they might experience drama in their lives and community
recognising how drama can show feelings and ideas people have about the world
asking questions about drama they experience
considering how drama communicates cultural knowledge in their own communities

AC9ADR2E02.minimum_width: Student identifies at least one occasion when First Nations Australians use drama and describes one way elements of drama are used in that context.
AC9ADR2E02.typical_width: Students explore when, where, how and why First Nations Australians use drama during cultural celebrations and significant occasions; they observe how elements (place, language, movement) are used; they explore how First Nations drama communicates knowledge of the local environment using resources co-created with First Nations communities.
wider: Students explore how First Nations Australians use drama to express connection to and responsibility for Country/Place — including seasonal knowledge and caring for country
Students co-create (with appropriate cultural guidance) a Welcome to Country or Acknowledgement of Country to perform before their drama class
Students engage with stories that communicate knowledge of the environment in their region, exploring how drama carries this knowledge
elaborations: exploring when, where, how and why First Nations Australians use drama during cultural celebrations
exploring First Nations Australians' use of drama to express connection to and responsibility for Country/Place
observing how elements such as place, language and movement are used in First Nations cultural expressions
exploring ways of communicating knowledge through stories from their region
co-creating a Welcome to Country or Acknowledgement of Country with cultural authority

AC9ADR2P01.minimum_width: Student performs drama in an informal setting to at least one audience member and responds to one reflection question about what the drama made them think or feel.
AC9ADR2P01.typical_width: Students retell familiar stories or share drama through acting in informal settings; they perform sequences including frozen images and transitions; they consider what they want audiences to think and feel; they reflect using structured questions about the experience as maker and audience.
wider: Students perform drama based on a community story, family experience, or exploration of First Nations Australians' connection to place
Students use digital recording to capture their performance and view it back, noticing what communicated well
Students perform in a wider informal context (another class, a school sharing event) adapting to a less familiar audience
elaborations: retelling a familiar story through acting and sharing with an audience
performing sequences of frozen images linked by transitions to communicate key scenes
reflecting using questions about what they want audiences to think, what the drama made them think about, and what they liked and why
